claims.value: outer segment discs: a stack of membrane-bound discs in the rod-shaped outer segment that hold the photopigment rhodopsin
claims.quote: The rod-shaped outer segments of the rod photoreceptor contain a stack of membrane-bound discs that contain the photosensitive pigment rhodopsin.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.quote: In rods the photopigment is in stacks of membranous disks separate from the outer cell membrane.

claims.value: rhodopsin: the rod photopigment, most sensitive to light at 498 nm
claims.quote: Rhodopsin, the photopigment in rods, is most sensitive to light at a wavelength of 498 nm.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.quote: The change in membrane potential alters the amount of neurotransmitter that the photoreceptor cells release onto bipolar cells in the outer synaptic layer.

claims.value: Photoreception happens in the specialized outer segment, while the inner segment houses the nucleus and the cell's other common organelles.
claims.quote: The inner segment contains the nucleus and other common organelles of a cell, whereas the outer segment is a specialized region in which photoreception takes place.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Rods are so sensitive to light that a single photon can lead to an action potential in the rod's corresponding retinal ganglion cell.
claims.quote: Rods are so sensitive to light that a single photon can result in an action potential from a rod’s corresponding RGC.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Strongly light-sensitive rods lie in the outer edges of the retina and detect dim light, serving mainly peripheral and night vision.
claims.quote: Rods are strongly photosensitive and are located in the outer edges of the retina. They detect dim light and are used primarily for peripheral and nighttime vision.

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Rods do not sense the color of light, so the low-light vision they provide is essentially in grayscale.
claims.quote: However, cones cannot react to low-intensity light, and rods do not sense the color of light. Therefore, our low-light vision is—in essence—in grayscale.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: In normal sunlight the rods' rhodopsin is constantly bleached while cones are active, but in a darkened room vision depends entirely on rods.
claims.quote: In normal sunlight, rhodopsin will be constantly bleached while the cones are active. In a darkened room, there is not enough light to activate cone opsins, and vision is entirely dependent on rods.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Activated rhodopsin starts a cascade that closes Na+ channels in the photoreceptor membrane, so the cell hyperpolarizes instead of depolarizing like most sensory neurons.
claims.quote: This isomerization of retinal activates the rhodopsin, starting a cascade of events that ends with the closing of Na+ channels in the membrane of the photoreceptor. Thus, unlike most other sensory neurons (which become depolarized by exposure to a stimulus) visual receptors become hyperpolarized

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Light changes a photoreceptor's membrane potential, which alters how much neurotransmitter it releases onto bipolar cells in the outer synaptic layer.
claims.quote: The photoreceptors (rods and cones) change their membrane potential when stimulated by light energy. The change in membrane potential alters the amount of neurotransmitter that the photoreceptor cells release onto bipolar cells in the outer synaptic layer.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

tier1.text: One of the two photoreceptor cell types of the vertebrate retina. In rods the photopigment is in stacks of membranous disks separate from the outer cell membrane. Rods are more sensitive to light than cones, but rod mediated vision has less spatial and temporal resolution than cone vision.
tier1.attribution: Definition from the Cell Ontology (CL 2026-06-08), CL:0000604. CC BY 4.0.
